definition: Hinder means to make progress harder — to slow, complicate, or set something back without necessarily stopping it altogether.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word hinder. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know hinder should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Fog hindered the search teams all morning, shrinking every sweep of the hillside to arm's length.
To delay is milder than to hinder: a delayed shipment arrives whole, just later, while a hindered one loses ground the whole way — slowed, complicated, and set back at every turn.
To thwart goes further than to hinder: a hindered plan still limps toward the finish, but a thwarted one is defeated outright — the goal is never reached at all.

To hamper is to restrict movement as if something were tangled around you — you are hampered by a heavy coat, by wet rope, by regulations that bind. Hinder is the broader word for any drag on progress, and it points at the result: a hindered effort ends up behind.

To impede is to slow something by putting an obstacle in its path — the word comes from Latin for shackling the feet. Hinder needs no obstacle in the road at all: fatigue, red tape, or plain bad luck can hinder you, because hinder measures the setback, not the barrier.

The expedition's real enemy was not the cold but the stamps: every border crossing demanded new paperwork, and each delay hindered the climbers just enough that they reached base camp three weeks behind the weather window.
Hinder names friction, not a wall.
The climbers were never stopped — they were slowed, complicated, and set back, which is exactly the word's range: making progress harder while it continues.
When something is halted outright, hinder understates it; when it merely arrives late but whole, hinder overstates it.
The word's home is the costly middle.
Hinder is the measured word for friction against progress — at home in reports, rulings, and post-game explanations.
It takes a direct object: rain hinders the harvest, debt hinders the recovery.
Reach for block or prevent when the thing never happens at all; hinder promises only difficulty and lost ground while the effort goes on.
In this unit, forestall acts early, before trouble starts — hinder drags at something already underway.

The volunteers who broke ground on the Maple Street garden in April expected an easy first season; the lot had sun, a fence, and a long waiting list of eager families.
Instead, nearly everything conspired to hinder them.
The soil turned out to be heavy clay that swallowed a full month of digging and amending.
Then a cracked main left the beds without water for two weeks in June, and deer found a gap under the fence the same night the tomatoes flowered.
None of it stopped the garden.
Seedlings went in late, volunteers hauled water in buckets, and a borrowed dog patrolled the rows at dusk.
The beds still filled by September, weeks behind the plan and lighter than hoped, but full -- a first season made harder at every turn, never halted.
